title: Does the cubic-residue graph on 127 vertices force a monochromatic triangle?
credit: Folkman (1970) existence; problem of bounding F_e(3,3;4): Erdős, Graham prize; G127 candidate suggested by G. Exoo; bounds by Radziszowski-Xu, Lange-Radziszowski-Xu, Bikov-Nenov.
premise_risks: Identification of G127 (Hill-Irwing graph) with the cubic-residue Cayley graph on Z_127 should be double-checked against Radziszowski-Xu 2007 (the K4-freeness and 42-regularity checks are consistent with it)
Largely a computational decision problem on one fixed graph; accepted because it is a recognised open problem in refereed literature
A negative answer (a good colouring) settles G127 but says little about F_e(3,3;4) itself
plain: Folkman showed that there are graphs with no 4 mutually adjacent vertices in which every red/blue colouring of the edges creates a single-coloured triangle. The fewest vertices such a graph can have, F_e(3,3;4), is only known to lie between 21 and 786. A natural candidate is the graph on the integers mod 127 that joins x and y when x - y is a nonzero cube mod 127; it has no 4 mutually adjacent vertices. Decide whether every red/blue colouring of its edges has a single-coloured triangle. A yes would show F_e(3,3;4) <= 127.
math: Let $G_{127}$ be the Cayley graph on $\mathbb Z_{127}$ with connection set $C=\{x^3: x\in\mathbb Z_{127}^{*}\}$ (a subgroup of order $42$ containing $-1$, so $G_{127}$ is a $42$-regular simple graph; it is $K_4$-free). Decide whether $G_{127}\to(3,3)^e$, i.e. whether every map $c:E(G_{127})\to\{0,1\}$ admits a triangle of $G_{127}$ whose three edges have the same colour. (Known: $21\le F_e(3,3;4)\le 786$; a positive answer gives $F_e(3,3;4)\le 127$.)
